claims.text: Adding approximately 1 at% yttrium during alloy processing will induce in-situ formation of Y2O3 precipitates.
The resulting Y2O3 precipitates will be uniformly dispersed and nanometer-scale.
The Y2O3 dispersion will improve high-temperature mechanical performance.
The yttrium addition and Y2O3 dispersion will preserve room-temperature mechanical properties.
Adding approximately 1 at% yttrium will leave alloy density nearly unchanged.
Heat treatment after melting and solidification can promote formation of fine Y2O3 precipitates in the yttrium-containing alloy.
Y2O3 dispersoids hinder dislocation motion at elevated temperatures.
Y2O3 dispersoids hinder grain-boundary sliding at elevated temperatures.
Hindering dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding will enhance creep resistance and yield strength.
The dispersoids will minimally affect room-temperature ductility.
Relative to an alloy processed without yttrium, the modified alloy will have a significantly lower creep rate at 800–1200 °C.
Relative to an alloy processed without yttrium, the modified alloy will have higher yield strength at 800–1200 °C.
Fine and uniform precipitate distribution is required for the proposed improvement.
Coarse or clustered precipitates may fail to provide the proposed performance improvement.
The hypothesis will be tested against a no-yttrium control using high-temperature creep and yield tests, room-temperature tensile tests, density measurements, and microscopy.
Failure to achieve a statistically significant high-temperature strength or creep improvement, or an adverse room-temperature-property or density change, is designated as a falsifying outcome.
